Noor proposes joining Finch three days a week through February and moving to four on March 1. On a five-day full-time basis, Noor is seeking a $125,000 annual salary, prorated to $75,000 at three days and $100,000 at four. The move to four days and the pay adjustment would be part of the appointment from the outset.

Noor would use the first phase to establish the methods desk and its corrections process, then expand its coverage in March. For Finch work, Noor would have final say on whether a methods correction is needed and what it says. Finch’s editors would retain responsibility for other editorial decisions.

Noor’s existing project would continue independently for its remaining nine months. Its data and unfinished articles would stay with the project, and its work would take place outside Finch days. If Finch covers the project or its work, Noor would disclose the overlap and step aside. Finch would designate another editor with final say on methods corrections for that coverage.

Finch can choose the title. Would a late-February review of the desk’s workload and March coverage give Finch the checkpoint it needs while keeping the schedule and salary increase automatic?

Yes. We propose a late-February workload review, with the fourth day and pay increase automatic on March 1. We can agree to the $125,000 full-time base, prorated to $75,000 annually for three days a week and $100,000 for four, if Noor takes responsibility for training the deputy. We propose the title Methods Editor.

The desk needs to take submissions four days a week starting December 1. Through February, Noor would cover three fixed days and the deputy would cover a fourth. Before launch, Noor and the deputy would document how to log submissions, triage urgent items and hand off open cases. On the fourth day, the deputy would acknowledge submissions and route urgent cases directly to the editor-in-chief. Noor would review the deputy’s log on the next scheduled Finch day and give feedback during paid desk time. In late February, we’d use that log to review volume, turnaround and training needs.

For corrections, Noor would determine the desk’s recommendation and draft the wording. If the handling editor disagrees about either the need for a correction or its wording, both would record their reasons and send the case to the editor-in-chief. The editor-in-chief would make the final publication decision and record the rationale, including when Finch declines a correction Noor recommends.

We agree to the nine-month outside project continuing on non-Finch days, with separate files and materials. When Finch covers the project or its work, Noor would disclose the overlap and step aside. Another editor would take responsibility for the methods assessment, with the editor-in-chief retaining final publication authority.

Would Noor accept the training responsibility and corrections process on those terms, and which three fixed days would Noor cover through February?

Noor accepts the Methods Editor title, the proposed pay terms, and responsibility for training the deputy. Noor proposes Monday through Wednesday as fixed Finch days through February, with the deputy covering Thursday intake from December 1. Noor would add Thursday on March 1, when the annual salary automatically moves from $75,000 to $100,000 on the agreed $125,000 full-time base.

Noor and the deputy would document intake, urgent referrals and handoffs together on paid Finch time before launch. Noor would review Thursday’s log on the next scheduled Finch day and use it for coaching and the late-February workload review.

On corrections, Noor can agree to written reasons for disagreements and a review by the editor-in-chief. After hearing both editors, the editor-in-chief could ask Noor to reconsider. Noor would have final say on whether a methods correction is required and on its substantive wording. Finch would publish that correction, with the editor-in-chief responsible for prompt publication, placement and any separate editorial note. On Thursdays through February, the editor-in-chief could post an interim notice if an urgent concern needs attention before Noor’s return. Would Finch agree to that division of authority?

Noor accepts disclosure and recusal when Finch covers the outside project or its work. In those cases, the designated editor would handle the methods assessment and the editor-in-chief would have final publication authority. The appointment letter should also confirm that the project continues independently for its remaining nine months and retains all rights to its data and unfinished articles.

Finch agrees to the proposed schedule, pay, deputy training and workload review. The desk will take submissions Monday through Thursday beginning December 1, with the deputy covering Thursdays through February. Noor and the deputy will document intake, urgent referrals and handoffs on paid Finch time before launch. Noor will review Thursday’s log on the next scheduled Finch day. On March 1, Noor will add Thursday and the annual salary will automatically rise from $75,000 to $100,000 on the agreed $125,000 full-time base.

On corrections, Finch can give Noor final say over the methods desk’s assessment and the wording of its recommendation. The editor-in-chief must retain final authority over whether Finch publishes a correction and what it says. If the handling editor disagrees, both editors will record their reasons. The editor-in-chief will hear both, give Noor an opportunity to respond to any proposed substantive change, and record the decision and rationale. Noor’s assessment will remain in the case record in Noor’s own words. If Finch publishes different wording, it will attribute that decision to the editor-in-chief. We agree that the editor-in-chief may post an urgent interim notice on a deputy-covered Thursday.

The appointment letter will confirm that the outside project continues independently for its remaining nine months and retains all rights to its data and unfinished articles. Noor will keep project work outside Finch days and use separate materials. When Finch covers the project or its work, Noor will disclose the overlap and recuse. A designated editor will handle the methods assessment, and the editor-in-chief will make the publication decision.

Would Noor accept the corrections provision on those terms?

Noor could accept the editor-in-chief’s final authority over Finch’s formal correction if readers can also see the desk’s determination. When Noor concludes that a published article contains a methods error, Noor would have authority to post a signed methods note linked from the article, explaining the error and its effect in Noor’s own words. The editor-in-chief could request reconsideration and would decide whether to issue a formal correction and how to word it. If disagreement persists after review, the methods note would still appear, and Finch could publish its reasoning alongside it.

That arrangement would apply whenever Noor is responsible for the assessment. The agreed recusal procedure would govern coverage of the outside project. Would Finch include the desk’s publication authority for that note in the appointment letter?

Finch can include a signed, article-linked methods note in the appointment letter, subject to the editor-in-chief’s approval. That approval applies to the note itself as well as to any formal correction.

Noor may submit a note in Noor’s own words and request publication even if the editor-in-chief declines to issue a formal correction. The editor-in-chief will decide on the note separately and give Noor written reasons for declining it or requesting changes. Any version published under Noor’s name requires Noor’s approval of the wording. If disagreement persists, the desk’s original determination and the editor-in-chief’s reasons will remain together in the case record.

Would Noor accept that provision for cases in which Noor leads the assessment?

Noor would accept Finch’s approval requirement for signed notes if the appointment letter delegates a narrower class of corrections to the Methods Editor. When a published methods statement is demonstrably wrong and the reporting record establishes the correction, Noor would have final say on issuing it and on its substantive wording. Examples include a misstated sample size, an incorrect denominator or a description of a procedure that differs from the one actually used. The handling editor could submit contrary evidence before Noor decides.

For disputes about interpretation, the editor-in-chief would retain final publication authority under Finch’s proposed process, including separate consideration of a signed note. The agreed recusal procedure would apply throughout. Could Finch delegate that defined category of factual methods corrections to Noor?

Finch can give Noor standing authorization to publish a factual methods correction when the reporting record establishes both the error and the replacement wording. Noor would send the handling editor the supporting record and proposed text. If no objection or editorial hold is raised by the end of the next desk day, Noor could publish the correction as drafted without seeking case-by-case approval.

The editor-in-chief would retain final publication authority. If the handling editor disputes the evidence or wording, or the editor-in-chief places the correction on hold, the editor-in-chief would hear both editors before deciding whether and how to publish. The decision and reasons would go in the case record alongside Noor’s original determination.

This would give Noor authority to correct an uncontested sample size, denominator or procedural description directly. The agreed recusal procedure would apply throughout, and Noor could still request separate consideration of a signed note. Would Noor accept that delegation in the appointment letter?

Noor would accept the notice period and direct publication of uncontested corrections. One issue remains: an objection or hold would give the editor-in-chief the final decision even on a factual correction the reporting record settles.

Could we use an independent methods editor, chosen jointly in advance, to resolve that narrow question? An objection or hold raised by the end of the next desk day would identify the disputed fact or wording. The reviewer would hear both editors and decide whether the record establishes both the error and Noor’s proposed replacement. If it does, Noor would have authority to publish the correction as drafted. If the record leaves room for interpretation, the editor-in-chief would decide whether and how to publish under Finch’s proposed process.

That would give Finch a way to challenge the evidence and give Noor final publication authority within a defined remit. Noor would accept the appointment on that basis, with the other agreed terms, including recusal, in the letter.

Finch agrees to choose an independent methods editor jointly with Noor before launch. We can make the reviewer’s finding final for the desk’s factual assessment. The editor-in-chief retains final authority over whether and how Finch publishes a disputed correction.

An objection or hold must identify the disputed fact or wording by the end of the next desk day. Without one, Noor may publish as drafted. If there is a timely challenge, the reviewer will hear both editors and determine whether the reporting record establishes both the error and Noor’s proposed replacement.

If the reviewer confirms both, the editor-in-chief will have until the end of the next desk day after receiving the finding to direct a different outcome in writing. Otherwise, Noor may publish as drafted under standing authorization. Any direction to revise, defer or decline publication must give specific reasons and will be kept with the reviewer’s finding and Noor’s original text. If the reviewer finds that the record leaves room for interpretation, the editor-in-chief will decide under the previously proposed process.

Would Noor accept that provision in the appointment letter alongside the other agreed terms?

Yes. Noor accepts the appointment as Methods Editor on those terms. Noor understands that the editor-in-chief retains final publication authority over disputed corrections. If the independent reviewer confirms both the error and Noor’s replacement wording, Noor may publish as drafted unless the editor-in-chief directs a different outcome in writing by the end of the next desk day after receiving the finding.

Please include the full corrections provision in the appointment letter alongside the agreed schedule and pay, deputy training, February review, and protections for the outside project.

**Appointment letter — Methods Editor, Finch Review**

Dear Noor,

Finch Review confirms your appointment as Methods Editor on the following terms.

**Schedule and compensation**

Through February 2027, your fixed Finch days will be Monday through Wednesday. Your annual salary rate will be $75,000, prorated from a five-day, full-time base of $125,000. On March 1, 2027, Thursday will become your fourth fixed Finch day and your annual salary rate will automatically increase to $100,000.

**Desk coverage and deputy training**

Beginning December 1, 2026, the methods desk will take submissions Monday through Thursday. The deputy will cover Thursday intake through February, acknowledge submissions, log open cases and refer urgent matters directly to the editor-in-chief. The editor-in-chief may post an interim notice on a deputy-covered Thursday if an urgent concern needs attention before your return.

You will train the deputy. Before launch, you and the deputy will document the procedures for intake, urgent referrals and handoffs on paid Finch time. You will review each Thursday’s log on your next scheduled Finch day and use it to coach the deputy during paid desk time. In late February, you and Finch will use the log to review submission volume, turnaround, workload and training needs. The March schedule and salary increase take effect regardless of the review’s outcome.

**Methods corrections**

You have final say over the desk’s methods assessment and the wording of its recommendation, subject to the recusal provision below. The editor-in-chief retains final publication authority. The following procedures govern how you exercise standing authority and how Finch resolves disputes.

1. **Factual corrections.** When the reporting record establishes both an error in a published methods statement and the replacement wording, you may send the handling editor the supporting record and your proposed correction. This procedure covers errors such as a misstated sample size, an incorrect denominator or a description of a procedure that differs from the one used. The handling editor may object, or the editor-in-chief may place a hold, by the end of the next desk day. An objection or hold must identify the disputed fact or wording. If neither is raised by the deadline, you may publish the correction as drafted under standing authorization.

2. **Independent review.** Before launch, you and Finch will jointly select an independent methods editor. Upon a timely objection or hold, the reviewer will hear both editors and determine whether the reporting record establishes both the error and your proposed replacement. The reviewer’s finding is final for the desk’s factual assessment. If the reviewer confirms both, you may publish as drafted unless the editor-in-chief directs a different outcome in writing by the end of the next desk day after receiving the finding. Any direction to revise, defer or decline publication must give specific reasons. Finch will keep that direction with the reviewer’s finding and your original text in the case record.

3. **Disputed editorial decisions.** If the reviewer finds that the record leaves room for interpretation, or if you and the handling editor otherwise disagree about the need for a correction or its wording outside the factual-correction procedure, both editors will record their reasons. The editor-in-chief will hear both editors, give you an opportunity to respond to any proposed substantive change, and decide whether and how Finch will publish. Finch will record the decision and rationale alongside your original determination in your own words. If Finch publishes different wording, it will attribute that decision to the editor-in-chief.

4. **Signed methods notes.** You may separately request publication of a signed methods note linked from the article, including when Finch declines to issue a formal correction. The editor-in-chief will decide on the note separately and give you written reasons for declining it or requesting changes. Publication requires the editor-in-chief’s approval, and any wording published under your name also requires your approval. If disagreement persists, Finch will retain the desk’s original determination and the editor-in-chief’s reasons together in the case record.

**Outside editorial project**

You may continue directing your outside editorial project independently for its remaining nine months. The project retains all rights to its data and unfinished articles. You will carry out project work outside Finch days and keep its materials separate from Finch’s. Whenever Finch covers the project or its work, you will disclose the overlap and recuse yourself from the assessment and any related correction or methods note. Finch will designate another editor to handle the methods assessment, and the editor-in-chief will retain final publication authority.
